full_judgment:
3. Petitioner as defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and after taking all the preliminary objections as to maintainability of the suit, it is her case that Basirullah sold 44 decimals of land by deed No.4330 dated 23-9-1946 to the predecessor of defendant No. 1. Rustam Mia, Sultan Ahmed, son of Basirullah, sold to Rustam Mian 33 decimals of land by deed No.6227 dated 1-12-1957. SA khatian No. 17 rightly recorded his name along with others, as such, he was a co-sharer in the suit land. Rustom Mian died leaving Makbul Ahmed and 8 sons, one daughter, Hajera Begum. Makbul Ahmed died leaving 4 sons including defendant Nos. l and 4. The heirs of Basirullah were also co-sharer in the suit jote. Khaiz Ahmed, son of Basirullah died leaving wife, Halima Begum and Rokeya Begum and others as 3 daughters, Jamaluddin and others as 3 sons. In this way defendant Nos.2-4 became owners in the suit jote and they have transferred the suit plot to defendant No.1 by ewaj deed No.517 dated 28-1-1999. Defendant No.1 become the owner in that land and possessing the land to the knowledge of the plaintiff since transfer. Plaintiff is not entitled to claim pre-emption as he is no way co-sharer in the suit jote. Moreover, defendant No. 17 added after he has filed Miscellaneous Case No.62 of 2007. She has obtained a compromise decree in terms of solenama against the ewaj deed in question hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 7. On the question of maintainability of the suit, learned Advocate relied on the case of Nuri Miah vs Ambica Singh and another, 34 Indian Cases-869 and also the case of Md Arshad Hussain vs The State of Bihar and others, judgment dated 22-4-2011 passed in Letters Patent Appeal No.313 of 2010. 

 9. Mr Khair Ezaz Maswood along with Mr AQM Shafiullah, learned Advocates, appearing for the opposite parties, submits that concurring findings of fact if not perverse, under section 151(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure this Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with those findings. Learned Advocate on the question of two judgments on same subject matter submits that judgment passed under section 96 of the Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not decree, it is order, other judgment passed on the instant suit, which being decree prevail over the judgment passed under State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and relied on the case of Mohammad Siddiq vs Ghasi Ram, AIR 1946 (Lahore) 322. 

 12. Learned Advocate on determination of co-tenancy relied on the case of Fatema Bibi vs Sree Manik Lal Samaddar, 1996 BLD (AD) 129 = 50 DLR (AD) 97. Learned Advocate on separation of jama relied on the case of Male Mohammad vs Hafez Abul Kalam, 6 BLC (AD) 83 and the case of Abdul Momin alias Tara Mian vs Mahfizur Rahman, 1 ADC 515. 

 14. On the question of defect of parties, Courts below concurrently found that plaintiff took all the step in getting the suit ready for hearing and defendant did not raise any objection specifically against defect of parties and did not supply any particulars of co-sharers, who are left out, found that the suit is not bad for defect of parties. On the question of limitation it appears that apparently the suit is barred by limitation as transfer was made on 28-1-1999 but the suit was filed on 9-6-2002. Section 245 of the Mohammadan Law prescribed period for filing suit is one year. It appears from the plaint that plaintiff went to village home, as for his profession he resides at Dhaka, on 15-3-2002. PWs. in chief as well as in their cross-examination stated that on 15-3-2002 there was admission of the plaintiff to pre-empt the case land. Courts below considered that it is on evidence that delivery of possession is made in 2002. As per section 245 of the Mohammadan Law the case is not barred by limitation as such it has been within the period of limitation i.e. within one year from the date of knowledge. On the vital question i.e. whether formalities of filing of the suit has been performed or not, Courts below found that plaintiff as per section 236 of Mullas Principles of Mohammadan Law per-formed both Talab-i-Mowasibat and Talab-i-Ishad. PWs. in their examination-in-chief and in their cross-examination fully corroborate that plaintiff performed all the formalities as per section 236 of the Mohammadan Law. The depositions of DWs. on this score are totally contradictory and not satisfactory On the question whether plaintiff is co-sharer or not, both the Courts below found from the history sheet and admitted by defendant that plaintiff is a co-sharer and entitled to pre-empt the case land. On the question of maintainability of the suit it appears that D.W.I in cross-examination admitted that plaintiff having performed all the formalities of Mohammadan Law, suit is maintainable. 

 15. On the question of which judgment will prevail., the Judgment under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or the instant judgment under the Mohammadan Law as pre-emption under section 96 State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is totally different for pre-emption under Mohammadan Law. This is the prime question to be answered. 

 22. A proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which though makes a formal expression of an adjudication conclusively determining the rights of the parties with regard to any matter in controversy, being not a suit as referred to in the definition of a decree in the Code of Civil Procedure, cannot be said to be a decree within the meaning of the definition of adecree given in the code as aforesaid. 

 29 Like section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, first class excludes second class and second excludes third class. In the case of two or more pre-emptors of the same class, they are entitled to equal shares of property in respect of pre-empted property. 

 30. As per section 24(10) of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and section 97(17) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, right of pre-emption under Mohammadan Law shall get preference as it lays down as 'Nothing in this section shall take away the right of pre-emption conferred on any person by the Mohammadan Law as such right is a personal right. 

 8. In Baillie's Digest of Muhammadan Law Part I, second Edition, at page 487, there is the following observation in which the law on the point is stated :— 

 "On getting the notice the petitioner made an application for pre-emption under S. 26-F, Tenancy Act, in the Court of Second Munsif at Krishnagar on 6th June 1934. The transferees, namely opposite parties 1 to 3 were made parties defendants to that application.While this application was pending Muhamad Soleman instituted in the same Court a suit to enforce the right which he had to pre-empt under the Mohammedan law. The landlord was made defendant 10. This suit for pre-emption and the application under section 26-F were heard together and one judgment was pronounced. At the date of the order, in Misc. Case No.42 of 1935 the right, title and interest in the holding had already vested in Mohamed Soleman by reason of the pre-emption decree in the suit. There was no right, title and interest left to opposite par-ties 1 to 3 on which the pre-emption order, if made under S. 26-F, sub-section (5), can operate. That is to my mind a difficulty in the way of the landlord in the present case. The title in the holding which formerly belonged to the Kolas has now vested in Mohamed Soleman. There can be no order for pre-emption against Mohamed Soleman by reason of the provision of S.26-F, sub-section (1), Clause (a) ." Wherein it is held that competition between the right given under Mohammadan Law and right created under statutes, the right under the former will prevail. If plaintiff of suit under Mohammadan Law, whether heard analogously, simultaneously or separately, succeed on merits the application under the provision of statutes should be dismissed." 

 39. As such we are of the view that the decision passed in the instant suit prevailed over the compromise order obtained in the miscellaneous case. In the present case, plaintiff did make the immediate demand, that is, he did perform the ceremony of talabe mowasibat immediately on coming to know of the sale and also talab-i-ishad in presence of witnesses, which the PWs univocally proved. Moreover, section 24(10) of Non Agricultural Tenancy Act and section 96(17) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act speak that right of pre-emption under Muhammadan Law shall prevail which cannot be defeated by these statutory laws. We find no substance in these rules.
